chapters.title: Chapter 3: Constructing and Testing a Factor Strategy

lessons.title: Combining Multiple Factors: Diversification Across Return Drivers

body.text: Chapter 2 ended with a warning: no single factor works all the time. This lesson is the answer. Combining factors is not just about smoothing returns, it is about finding the stock that is cheap and improving, not merely cheap, the one the market has not fully rewarded on more than one dimension at once.

children.text: You can now build a single-factor score, backtest it honestly, and turn it into a real portfolio. This final lesson closes the loop: how to combine several factors deliberately, the two structurally different ways to do it, the diversification math behind why it works, and a worked example showing exactly how a stock's ranking can shift once you stop looking at value in isolation.
Two Ways to Combine Factors: Mix vs Integrate

There are two structurally different ways to run a multi-factor strategy, and they are not the same thing wearing different names. A mixed, or 'sleeve', approach builds separate single-factor portfolios, a value portfolio, a momentum portfolio, a quality portfolio, and allocates capital across them, commonly in equal parts. An integrated approach instead computes one blended composite score per stock, averaging its value, momentum, and quality z-scores together first, and only then ranks and selects based on that single combined number.

cells: Separate single-factor portfolios, combined at the allocation level
One composite score per stock, combined at the signal level before ranking
No, a stock strong on only one factor gets the same treatment within its sleeve as one strong on several
Yes, a stock that scores well on multiple factors simultaneously rises to the top of the blended ranking
High, each sleeve's contribution to performance is easy to isolate and explain
Lower, harder to cleanly attribute overall performance back to any one factor
Investors who want to control exposure to each factor individually
Investors chiefly interested in the single best-scoring stocks overall, regardless of which factor drives each pick

children.text: The Diversification Math: Why Combining Factors Smooths Returns

Chapter 2 argued qualitatively that different factors respond to different macro regimes and are therefore imperfectly correlated. Standard portfolio theory quantifies exactly how much that imperfect correlation helps.

body.caption: Two-factor portfolio variance: combining factors with correlation below 1 reduces total volatility below a simple weighted average

children.text: Take a hypothetical value strategy with 15% annualised volatility and a hypothetical momentum strategy with 18% annualised volatility, historically correlated at around minus 0.3, consistent with Chapter 2's observation that value and momentum often move in opposite directions across the cycle. A naive weighted average of the two volatilities, blended 50-50, would suggest 16.5% volatility. Plugging the actual numbers into the formula above tells a different story.

stats.label: Naive weighted average
stats.context: If correlation were assumed to be +1

stats.label: Actual combined volatility
stats.context: Using correlation of -0.3, from the formula above

children.text: A 50-50 blend of these two hypothetical strategies would carry roughly 9.8% volatility, meaningfully below either factor's standalone volatility, purely because their negative correlation lets losses in one partially offset gains, or losses, in the other. This is the entire mathematical case for combining factors: it is not that combining necessarily raises the average return, it is that imperfect correlation lowers risk for a given level of expected return, improving the strategy's risk-adjusted return.
Worked Example: Blending Value and Momentum at the Stock Level

Return to the six hypothetical stocks from Chapter 3's first lesson. Each already has a value composite score. Add a hypothetical momentum z-score for each, and build an integrated score by averaging the two.

body.caption: Integrating value and momentum changes the ranking (hypothetical companies, continued from Lesson 1)

body.text: Stock A was the clear value-only winner, but its weak momentum drags it down to fourth once the two signals are integrated. Stock F, a mediocre value-only pick in fourth place, jumps to third on the strength of its momentum. Stocks B and E, strong but not exceptional on either single factor, end up tied at the top of the integrated ranking precisely because they are the only two stocks that score reasonably well on both dimensions at once. This is exactly what an integrated multi-factor approach is built to find, and exactly what a single-factor value screen, or a value sleeve run alongside a separate momentum sleeve, would never surface as clearly.

children.text: A Note on Factor Timing: Why This Course Doesn't Recommend It

Everything in this lesson assumes a static, always-diversified blend across factors. Some practitioners instead attempt factor timing, tactically overweighting whichever factor they expect to outperform next based on the macro regime. Whether factor timing genuinely adds value net of costs is a contested question in quant finance, with credible arguments and evidence on multiple sides, and it is a meaningfully harder problem than simply staying diversified. Given Chapter 2's lesson on performance chasing, and how easily 'timing' shades into simply extrapolating whichever factor did well recently, this course's default recommendation is a static, diversified multi-factor blend, treating factor timing as an advanced, unresolved research question rather than a reliable technique to lean on by default.

body.title: Mixed vs Integrated: Which Approach Fits the Mandate?
body.scenario: An investment committee wants a factor strategy but has two, somewhat conflicting requirements: they want to be able to clearly report to their board exactly how much of the fund's performance came from value versus momentum versus quality each quarter, but they also want the strategy to concentrate capital in the stocks with the strongest overall combination of signals rather than spreading evenly across separate sleeves.
body.prompt: Which of the two combination approaches from this lesson better satisfies each requirement, and is there a genuine tension between the two goals here?
body.modelAnswer: There is a real tension. The mixed, sleeve-based approach is what satisfies the first requirement: because each factor is run as a separate portfolio, its individual contribution to overall performance can be cleanly isolated and reported. The integrated, signal-blend approach is what satisfies the second requirement: by combining scores at the stock level before ranking, it naturally concentrates capital in stocks with strong combined signals, exactly the outcome the committee says it wants, but at the cost of much murkier performance attribution, since a single integrated portfolio's return cannot be cleanly split back into 'how much came from value' versus 'how much came from momentum.' The committee will need to prioritise one goal over the other, or accept a compromise, such as running an integrated core strategy alongside separate, smaller single-factor tracking sleeves purely for attribution reporting purposes.

body.title: Test Yourself: What Correlation Does for Diversification
body.question: Using the two-factor variance formula from this lesson, what would happen to the combined portfolio's volatility if value and momentum were perfectly positively correlated (correlation of +1) instead of -0.3, holding the individual volatilities and weights the same?
options: The combined volatility would be unaffected by the change in correlation
The combined volatility would fall further below the naive weighted average
The combined volatility would rise to exactly equal the simple weighted average of the two individual volatilities, eliminating the diversification benefit
The combined volatility would become negative, which is not mathematically possible
body.explanation: When correlation equals +1, the two-factor variance formula simplifies algebraically so that the combined volatility exactly equals the simple weighted average of the individual volatilities, in this case 16.5%. Diversification benefit specifically comes from correlation being below +1; at exactly +1, there is no benefit left to capture.

body.title: Vocabulary Check: Terms From This Lesson

cards.definition: Combining factors by running separate single-factor portfolios and allocating capital across them, prioritising transparency and attribution over concentrating in multi-factor overlap.
Combining factors by averaging each stock's z-scores across factors into one composite score before ranking, concentrating capital in stocks that score well on multiple factors at once.
The reduction in combined portfolio volatility that arises specifically from combining return streams with a correlation below +1, quantified by the two-factor variance formula.
Tactically overweighting whichever factor is expected to outperform next based on the macro regime, a contested and harder-to-execute alternative to a static, diversified factor blend.

body.text: The volatility figures, correlation assumption, and momentum z-scores used in this lesson's worked examples are entirely hypothetical, chosen only to illustrate the underlying mathematics and mechanics. This is not investment advice or a recommendation regarding the actual historical or expected volatility or correlation of any real factor strategy.

points: A mixed (sleeve) approach combines factors at the portfolio allocation level, prioritising transparency and clean performance attribution
An integrated (signal-blend) approach combines factors at the individual stock score level, concentrating capital in stocks that score well on multiple factors simultaneously

The two-factor variance formula shows precisely why combining imperfectly correlated factors reduces portfolio volatility below a naive weighted average, with the benefit disappearing entirely at a correlation of +1

In the worked example, integrating value and momentum scores meaningfully reshuffled the ranking, demoting the pure value winner and promoting stocks strong on both dimensions, exactly the effect a single-factor screen cannot capture
Factor timing, tactically overweighting an expected-to-outperform factor, remains a genuinely contested technique and risks the same performance-chasing trap covered in Chapter 2
A static, diversified multi-factor blend, mixed or integrated depending on the mandate's priorities, is this course's default recommendation over attempting to time which single factor will work next
